content: Combined injectable contraceptives (CICs) are monthly injections that contain a combination of progesterone and estradiol, designed to inhibit fertility. These contraceptives are marketed under brand names such as Cyclofem, Novafem, Mesigyna, and Lunelle. On October 5, 2000, the pharmaceutical company Pharmacia received FDA approval for Lunelle™, a monthly contraceptive injection. In April 2003, Pharmacia was acquired by Pfizer, the company that also manufactures Depo-Provera. CICs are administered via intramuscular injection into one of three sites: the deltoid muscle, the gluteus maximus, or the anterior thigh. Ideally, the injection should be given every 28 to 30 days, although studies have shown that it remains effective for up to 33 days. The most common side effects associated with CICs are menstrual irregularities, particularly during the first three to six months of use. The formulations of these contraceptives vary by brand: Lunelle contains 25 mg of medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) and 5 mg of estradiol cypionate (E2C). Cyclofem contains 25 mg of depomedroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) and 5 mg of estradiol cypionate. Mesigyna contains 50 mg of norethisterone enanthate (NET EN) and 5 mg of estradiol valerate. Deladroxate contains 150 mg of dihydroxyprogesterone acetophenide and 10 mg of estradiol enanthate.
